passage: Thursday night in the hostel common room, three friends and one visitor had their laptops open. Varun read out a message from his professor: she wanted to talk about his essay, because parts of it sounded machine-written. His stomach dropped. Two paragraphs had been drafted by a chatbot and then tidied by him, so he decided to bring his notes and chat history to the meeting and ask what the department allowed. Jahnavi barely looked up. She was typing to her AI companion about a rotten day, and it answered warmly every time, never tired, never critical. "Easier than ringing anyone," she said, then added, "though I haven't replied to Nisha in two weeks." Yusuf pasted a chatbot's summary of a tax rule into his slides. "It sounds so sure," he said, then frowned. "I'll find the real source before I present." From the sofa, Ritu scrolled job listings for her design course and read one aloud that mentioned automation. "Will there be any work for me at all?" she asked. 😟

qa.q: What did Varun's professor say about his essay?
qa.a: The professor said parts of it sounded machine-written and wanted to talk about it.

qa.q: How do Varun's plan for the meeting and Yusuf's plan for his slides show a similar careful approach to AI tools?
qa.a: Both take responsibility for what the AI produced: Varun will bring his notes and chat history and be honest about his process, while Yusuf will look for the real source instead of accepting a confident answer.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he read the professor's message, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt exposed and anxious; his stomach dropped, and he quickly began planning what to bring to the meeting.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do to keep her human friendships growing alongside her companion?
qa.a: She could reply to Nisha and arrange to talk or meet, enjoying the companion's comfort without letting it replace her friends. 🙂

grounding: Four students at one hostel table show different stances toward AI tools: suspicion from a professor, comfort from a companion, over-trust of confident answers, and fear about jobs.

passage: Anand, the team lead, closed the Monday review with a smile. "Nobody is as dependable as you, Tushar," he said, and dropped two more client accounts on Tushar's plate. Tushar nodded, though he had been finishing reports at midnight for a month. That evening he ate in silence and snapped when the tap dripped. Vikas, his partner, felt the chill but did not take it personally. "I miss you," he said softly. "Could we keep Sunday breakfast, phones away?" Tushar agreed, guiltily. A few days later his friend Ritu caught him yawning over a lunch he barely touched. "You look flattened. Go home and rest," she said. He almost laughed it off, then only said, "Yeah. Okay. A walk after work, maybe?" By the lake he admitted that most mornings felt hollow. The next week he sat in a clinic and told the doctor everything: the poor sleep, the skipped meals, the low mood, the late nights he had been hiding. The doctor listened and set up follow-up visits. Back at work, Tushar wrote down every task he held and asked Anand which ones mattered most.

qa.q: What did Anand do at the end of the Monday review?
qa.a: He said nobody is as dependable as Tushar and dropped two more client accounts on his plate.

qa.q: How did Vikas's response to Tushar's exhaustion differ from Anand's?
qa.a: Anand praised Tushar's dependability while adding more accounts, whereas Vikas said softly that he missed him and suggested keeping Sunday breakfast, caring for Tushar rather than using his effort.

qa.q: How was Tushar likely feeling when he agreed to the Sunday breakfast, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was probably guilty and worn down; he agreed guiltily right after snapping at home and eating in silence.

qa.q: What could Tushar keep doing to stay well after the clinic visit?
qa.a: He could keep small rituals like Sunday breakfast and lakeside walks, attend the follow-up visits, and keep asking Anand which tasks matter most. 🙂

grounding: One overworked man meets a boss who adds load, a partner who gently reaches out, a friend who notices, and a doctor he is honest with.

passage: Six-year-old Vaibhav sat on the doorstep holding Nani's shawl. "Who will tell me the crocodile story now?" he asked. His mother, Bidisha, said, "Nani has died, and she cannot come back. I miss her too." He asked again the next morning, and she answered again in the same plain words. On Sunday the house filled with relatives. Aunties chopped vegetables in the kitchen, uncles sat on the floor reading prayers, and some people cried while others passed around tea. His father, Tejas, carried in a big pot of rice. Vaibhav did not follow the words, but he leaned against his uncle's arm and stayed. Later he found the photo album and stopped at Dada, who had died the winter before and used to keep toffees in his pocket for him. "Dada gave me sweets," he said, smiling and wiping his eyes. Bidisha helped him draw Dada holding a giant toffee. That night, in the dark, he whispered, "Mummy, will you die too?" Bidisha lay down beside him. "Everybody dies one day, but most people live a very long time. Papa and I are here, and we will always look after you." He held her hand until he fell asleep.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav holding when he sat on the doorstep?
qa.a: He was holding Nani's shawl.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's feelings at night differ from what he felt looking at Dada's photo, and what helped each?
qa.a: Looking at Dada's photo he felt warm and sad together, and drawing Dada with a toffee helped; at night he was frightened and asked if Mummy would die, and calm honest words that most people live a long time helped.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been feeling when he whispered his question in the dark?
qa.a: He was probably frightened; he asked in the dark and held Bidisha's hand until he fell asleep.

qa.q: Which choice by Bidisha helped Vaibhav with his grief, and why?
qa.a: She answered his repeated questions in the same plain words, so he could ask again and feel safe and looked after.

grounding: A young child's grief for a grandparent, his night-time fear, a warm memory of another grandparent, and the family gathering that holds him.

passage: After Pallavi moved to a new school, lunch was the loneliest hour. At night a stranger in a music group chat was kind to her, always asking about her day. "Don't mention me to anyone," the stranger wrote one week. "Nobody would understand us." Devika noticed Pallavi hiding her phone and jumping at every buzz. "You've gone quiet," she said. "I'm not cross, just worried. Want to show me?" Pallavi did. The stranger had asked for a picture and, once she sent it, wrote that it would go to her whole class unless she sent more. Devika did not scold. "This isn't your fault," she said. "Don't reply, don't pay, don't send anything. Let's save every message." They took screenshots together, and before the bell Devika walked her to the counsellor. The counsellor sat with Pallavi, told her the shame belonged to the person making threats, and called her parents and the cybercrime helpline that same afternoon. Kunal, at the next table, had overheard. He had been chatting with a gaming friend for months and badly wanted to meet. That evening he told his mother, who said they could meet at a busy cafe with her sitting nearby. When the friend replied, "Come alone and keep it secret," Kunal stopped replying.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi meet the stranger who was kind to her?
qa.a: She met the stranger in a music group chat.

qa.q: How did Kunal's handling of his online friend differ from what happened to Pallavi with her stranger?
qa.a: Kunal told his mother, planned a busy cafe with her nearby, and stopped replying when asked for secrecy; Pallavi hid her phone and was pressured to send a picture, and only became safer when Devika helped her save the messages and see the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have felt in the days before she showed Devika, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was probably afraid and anxious, since she hid her phone and jumped at every buzz.

qa.q: What small steps did Devika take that made it safer for Pallavi to get help?
qa.a: She listened without scolding, said it was not Pallavi's fault, told her not to reply or pay, saved the messages, and walked her to the counsellor.

grounding: Four teens meet an online stranger in different ways: curiosity about meeting, loneliness, a friend's protective concern, and coercion with a threat.

passage: Vikas had one new rule: both boys home before sunset, since a scooter had skidded near the market. Francis, fourteen, went straight to work. His eyes filled, his voice wobbled, and he called his father the best in the street. It worked once, and afterwards the sweetness sat in his mouth like something borrowed. Anand, sixteen, went the loud way. "You treat us like babies!" he shouted, and his bedroom door rattled. The next evening he tried again, quietly. "The team practises at the ground then, and I need to be there. I know the road scares you. Could I message when I leave and when I arrive?" Vikas said he would think. Francis, meanwhile, refused to speak at dinner for three days and left his maths book shut, as though that would punish anyone. On the fourth night Anand sat beside his father. "What exactly are you afraid will happen?" Vikas rubbed his forehead. "A truck. Bad company. People talking if you are out late." "Then let's fix those," Anand said. "Try me for two weeks." Vikas looked at the boys, and slowly nodded.

qa.q: What happened near the market that led to Vikas's new rule?
qa.a: A scooter had skidded near the market.

qa.q: How did Francis's first move differ from Anand's second try, and which fits better with earning trust?
qa.a: Francis's eyes filled and he called his father the best in the street, and it worked once, but the sweetness felt borrowed; Anand said he needed to be at the ground, knew the road scares his father, and offered to message when he leaves and arrives, so the quiet honest try fits better with trust.

qa.q: How was Francis feeling during the three silent days at dinner?
qa.a: He was resentful and angry, which he showed by refusing to speak and leaving his maths book shut.

qa.q: What could Francis try instead of tears or silence?
qa.a: He could say calmly what the rule costs him and ask for a trial, as Anand did, so his father can see he takes the fear seriously.

grounding: One household shows four teen stances toward a parent's rule: manipulation, an argument, silent resentment, and asking what the parent's fear is.

passage: Anirban waved his phone at Ira. "Come to the rally on Saturday, or you're not really with us," he said, and urged her to repost a furious slogan. Ira had not read the petition behind it. She read it that night, agreed with half, and shared only the part she could stand behind. At dinner she asked her mother, Madhuri, about Saturday. "No," Madhuri said at once. "Crowds turn, and I would be sick with worry." Ira felt her ears burn but said, "I hear you. Could I write letters to the council and sell bookmarks to pay for banners instead?" Madhuri thought, then nodded. In the corridor a classmate laughed. "Posters won't save a lake, Ira. Pointless." Ira took a breath and pulled out her printed figures. "Last time, forty families wrote in and the council changed the drain plan. It's slow, but it moves." That night her stomach twisted at the thought of a teacher calling the students troublemakers, or police turning up. She told Madhuri, and they read together what the rules for peaceful gatherings allowed. Being scared, Madhuri said, did not make anyone a coward.

qa.q: What did Ira offer her mother instead of going to the rally?
qa.a: She offered to write letters to the council and sell bookmarks to pay for banners.

qa.q: How did Ira handle Anirban's pressure differently from her mother's refusal?
qa.a: With Anirban she read the petition first and shared only what she believed; with Madhuri she listened and offered safer ways to help, like letters and bookmarks.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling that night when she thought about teachers and police?
qa.a: She felt afraid of the consequences; her stomach twisted, and she chose to tell Madhuri.

qa.q: What could Ira do next to keep helping the cause?
qa.a: She could keep writing letters and selling bookmarks, and keep gathering facts for anyone who calls it pointless. 🙂

grounding: One teen meets peer pressure, a parent's ban, a sceptical classmate and her own fear while deciding how to take part in a cause.
